title: You Dont Have a Time Problem You Have a Decision Backlog
author: Kelly McGinnis
summary: Kelly McGinnis argues that leaders who feel perpetually behind are not suffering from a time problem but a decision backlog -- the accumulation of unmade decisions that each charge ongoing interest in the form of team stagnation, wasted effort, eroded trust, and depleted mental bandwidth. She identifies three categories of decision debt: decisions the leader has outgrown (now belonging to someone else), decisions that were never theirs in the first place (absorbed from a team member's question), and decisions they are actively avoiding because the answer is uncomfortable. The article prescribes a ten-minute Friday audit: write down every unmade decision, then ask three questions: is this actually mine, do I already know the answer, and what is the one piece of information I need to decide? McGinnis argues that the leaders who rise are not the ones who make decisions faster but the ones who get better at deciding which decisions are theirs to make -- the quiet transition from making more decisions to making fewer, better ones.
points: Every unmade decision is a small, persistent draw on a leader's capacity -- it is not neutral; it charges interest in the form of team stagnation, wasted effort, and the erosion of trust from people who were told 'soon' and are starting to wonder if soon means anything.

Three categories of decision debt require different treatments: decisions the leader has outgrown (mechanically delegate), decisions that were never theirs in the first place (return them), and decisions being actively avoided because the answer is uncomfortable (these are the most expensive).

The Friday audit -- ten minutes, three questions per item -- clears the backlog and, over time, changes how a leader operates the following week as they begin to feel the cost of an unmade decision the moment it lands.

Senior leadership is distinguished not by faster decision-making but by greater selectivity -- the shift from making more decisions to making fewer, better ones is one of the quiet transitions most leaders never make.

When a leader says 'let me think about it' and does not come back, they have made a decision: they decided to keep the question open, decided the cost of holding it was lower than the cost of making it, and decided to make their team wait.
quotes: For years, I couldn't pick a restaurant on a Friday night. Not because I didn't have opinions about restaurants. By Friday evening, I'd have had a full week of leading a complex business and a complex team. So when my husband would ask me where I wanted to go for dinner, I'd feel something close to panic.

I was carrying a backlog of unmade decisions from the week, and by Friday evening, there was nothing left in me to decide anything else. I had exhausted my capacity to choose at work. What I was bringing home to my family and friends was the scraps.
Every unmade decision is a small, persistent draw on your capacity. It isn't neutral. It charges interest.
When you tell someone, 'Let me think about it,' and then you don't come back to it for two weeks, you've made a decision. It's just not the one you intended to create.
The decision you avoided is not the one you escaped. It's the one you made by default. And usually, by default, you have created the most unfavorable version of it.
The leaders who rise aren't the ones who get faster at making decisions. They're the ones who get better at deciding which decisions are theirs to make.

The leader who tries to make every decision in their orbit is not more rigorous. They are simply unwilling to admit that their attention is finite, and they're paying the price of that refusal in everything else they touch.
